justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, anchored around a current price near $14.02. At the one-day horizon, the estimate stays close to the last observed price because intraday mean reversion tendencies and the absence of major scheduled catalysts suggest little directional pressure. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $14.10, reflecting a mild bullish bias consistent with whatever near-term momentum or sector trend was present at the time of the forecast. The one-month estimate of $14.25 continues that gentle upward slope, essentially assuming a continuation of modest positive drift without a strong fundamental catalyst forcing a large repricing in either direction.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is consistent with standard volatility scaling — uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 74 basis points, reflecting tight short-term price clustering typical of a low-to-moderate volatility asset. By one week, that range expands to about 180 basis points, incorporating the possibility of earnings-adjacent moves, macro data releases, or sector rotation. At one month, the interval balloons to roughly 340 basis points, acknowledging that over four weeks, a wide range of macroeconomic, sector-specific, and idiosyncratic developments could materially shift the price.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include unexpected earnings surprises or guidance revisions if this is an equity, sharp moves in correlated macro variables such as interest rates or commodity prices, and broader market regime shifts like a sudden risk-off episode or a credit event elsewhere in the financial system. Liquidity shocks or large institutional positioning changes — particularly if this is a smaller-cap or thinly traded instrument — could also produce gap moves that breach the outer bounds of the intervals.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals are calibrated under relatively normal market conditions, and fat-tail events are structurally underweighted in any forecast like this. A genuine macro shock, geopolitical escalation, or company-specific negative news could easily produce a move of 15–25% or more within the one-month window, well outside the stated range. Conversely, a strongly positive surprise could drive prices meaningfully above the upper bound as well.
